query: In Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs phase stability and why, with relevance to retaining desirable combinations of high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness? Specify a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries of the hypothesis, supporting prior evidence, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The phase stability of Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys is primarily governed by the degree of atomic size mismatch and the resulting lattice strain, which in turn controls whether the alloy remains in a disordered, entropy‐stabilized state or undergoes phase segregation into ordered intermetallic compounds.
generation.material_initial_state: A nominal single-phase, disordered Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloy with a composition near the optimal balance of atomic sizes and configurational entropy.
generation.intervention: Systematically vary the alloy composition (for example, by incrementally increasing or decreasing the Al content or adjusting one of the other elemental proportions) to modulate the atomic size mismatch and associated lattice strain.
generation.conditions: Conduct controlled heat treatments and annealing experiments under identical thermal histories while testing mechanical performance at high temperatures, under radiation exposure, and at cryogenic conditions. Use identical cooling rates to minimize other variables.
generation.structural_mediator: Local lattice distortions and strain fields that emerge because of atomic size differences, which can promote the nucleation of short-range ordering in the form of intermetallic phases.
generation.mechanism: When the atomic size mismatch (and thus lattice strain) is below a certain threshold, the configurational entropy dominates, maintaining a single-phase disordered structure that provides high toughness, environmental resistance, and radiation tolerance. Exceeding this threshold increases the strain energy enough to drive a phase transition, causing the formation of ordered intermetallic phases that degrade properties like high-temperature strength and cryogenic toughness.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloy samples with controlled compositions that maintain atomic size mismatch below the critical threshold will exhibit a stable, disordered microstructure with retained high-temperature strength, radiation tolerance, environmental resistance, and cryogenic toughness. In contrast, samples with greater mismatch will show evidence of secondary ordered phases (e.g., B2-type ordering) along with reduced performance in these key properties relative to the baseline.
generation.baseline: A standard Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni composition with moderate Al content representing the optimal balance between atomic size mismatch and high configurational entropy, resulting in a single-phase disordered structure.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies specifically to the Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloy system near the composition range where the balance between lattice strain and configurational entropy is critical. It may not extend to compositions with very high or very low Al (or other element) content or to other high-entropy alloy systems with significantly different atomic size distributions.
generation.uncertainty: The precise threshold of atomic size mismatch that triggers phase segregation, as well as the quantitative extent to which lattice strain influences property degradation, remains to be determined. Additionally, potential synergistic effects of minor compositional fluctuations are not fully understood.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloy samples with deliberate incremental variations in atomic size mismatch (e.g., by modifying the Al content or substituting one element with another of a slightly different atomic radius). Subject all samples to an identical thermal treatment schedule and evaluate microstructural changes using techniques such as X-ray diffraction (XRD) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM). Simultaneously, perform mechanical tests (e.g., tensile tests at high temperature, radiation exposure tests, and cryogenic toughness measurements).
measurements: Phase identification using XRD and TEM to detect the onset of any ordered intermetallic phases.
Mechanical property assessment (tensile strength, toughness) at high, moderate, and cryogenic temperatures.
Radiation damage resistance evaluation under controlled irradiation conditions.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if increasing the atomic size mismatch (as measured by compositional modifications) does not lead to a detectable transition from a disordered to an ordered microstructure, or if the appearance of any detectable secondary phases does not correlate with a measurable degradation in high-temperature strength, radiation tolerance, or cryogenic toughness relative to the baseline alloy.
